title: Eyes and Screens
summary: How your eyes see, why long screen time can leave them tired and dry, and simple habits like the 20-20-20 rule and outdoor play that protect them.
poll: Kids should have a time limit for using screens every day.

versions.title: Eyes and Screens
versions.text:
Do you like to play games on a screen? Lots of kids do. But your eyes need care.

Here is how you see. Light goes in the dark dot in your eye. Then it hits the back. A note goes to your brain. Now you see!

To see a thing up close, your eyes must focus. Small parts in the eye pull hard. A screen is close. So your eyes work hard the whole time. They get tired. Your head may hurt.

When you look at a screen, you blink less. Then your eyes get dry. They may itch.

Here is a good rule. Each 20 minutes, look at a thing far off. Look for 20 seconds. This lets your eyes rest.

Play out in the sun, too. Kids who play out a lot are less likely to need glasses.

Do not use a screen just as you go to bed. Its bright light can keep you up.

Screens are fine. Just give your eyes a break!

versions.title: Eyes and Screens
versions.text:
Do you like to watch shows or play games on a screen? Most kids do. But your eyes need care when you use one.

Here is how your eyes work. Light goes in through the black dot in the middle of each eye. It lands at the back of the eye. Then a message goes to your brain, and you see.

To see things up close, your eyes must focus. Tiny parts inside the eye pull hard to do this. A screen is close to your face. So your eyes work hard the whole time. They can get tired. Your head may hurt, too.

When you stare at a screen, you blink less. Then your eyes can get dry and itchy.

Try this rule. Every 20 minutes, look at something far away. Look for 20 seconds. This gives your eyes a rest.

Play outside, too. Kids who spend lots of time outside are less likely to need glasses to see far away.

Turn off screens well before bed. Their bright light can make it hard to sleep.

Screens are not bad. Just give your eyes a break!

Screens are not bad. Just use them wisely and give your eyes a break.

versions.title: Eyes and Screens
versions.text:
Phones, tablets, and TVs are everywhere. Lots of kids spend hours each day looking at a screen for school, games, and shows. Your eyes need care when you do this.

First, it helps to know how your eyes work. Light enters through the black dot in the middle of each eye. A clear part behind it bends the light so that it lands on the back of the eye. Then a message travels to your brain, and you see a picture.

To see things up close, your eyes must focus. Tiny muscles inside each eye squeeze to make this happen. Because a screen is close to your face, these muscles work hard the whole time. After a while, your eyes feel tired. Your head might hurt, or things may look blurry.

When you stare at a screen, you also blink less than usual. Blinking spreads tears that keep your eyes wet. With less blinking, your eyes can become dry and itchy.

Eye doctors suggest the 20-20-20 rule. Every 20 minutes, look at something about 6 meters away for 20 seconds. This lets your eyes rest.

Playing outside every day helps, too. Kids who spend more time outside are less likely to need glasses to see far away.

Finally, turn off screens an hour before bed, because their bright light can make it hard to fall asleep.

Screens are useful tools. Just use them well and give your eyes breaks.

versions.title: Eyes and Screens: Giving Your Eyes a Break
versions.text:
Phones, tablets, computers, and TVs are part of daily life. Many students spend several hours a day looking at screens for schoolwork, games, and videos. Screens are useful, but your eyes need care when you use them.

First, it helps to know how your eyes work. Light enters through the pupil, the black opening in the center of each eye. A clear lens behind it bends the light so that it lands on the retina, a thin layer at the back of the eye. The retina turns the light into signals and sends them to your brain, which creates the picture you see.

To see things up close, your eyes must focus. Tiny muscles inside each eye squeeze to change the shape of the lens. Because a screen is close to your face, these muscles keep working the whole time. After a while, you may feel eye strain. Your eyes feel tired, your head may ache, and things can look blurry.

When you stare at a screen, you also blink less than usual. Blinking spreads tears that keep your eyes wet, so less blinking can make them dry and itchy.

Eye doctors suggest the 20-20-20 rule. Every 20 minutes, look at something about 6 meters away for 20 seconds. Looking far away lets the muscles relax.

Time outdoors matters, too. Many more children are nearsighted today, which means they see close things clearly but far things look blurry. Studies show that kids who play outside every day are less likely to become nearsighted.

Finally, turn off screens about an hour before bed, because bright light can make it harder to fall asleep.

Screens are helpful tools. Just use them wisely and give your eyes regular breaks.

versions.title: Eyes and Screens: Protecting Your Vision in a Digital World
versions.text:
Phones, tablets, computers, and televisions have become an essential part of daily life, and many students now spend several hours each day looking at screens for schoolwork, entertainment, and communication. Screens are valuable tools, but your eyes require special attention when you use them for extended periods.

To understand why, it helps to know how your eyes function. Light enters through the pupil, the dark opening in the center of each eye, and a transparent lens bends that light so that it lands precisely on the retina, a thin layer of sensitive cells lining the back of the eye. The retina converts the light into electrical signals, which travel along the optic nerve to your brain, where they are assembled into the image you see.

To see objects up close, your eyes must focus, so tiny muscles inside each eye contract to adjust the shape of the lens. Because a screen is typically held close to your face, these muscles remain active the entire time. Eventually, you may experience digital eye strain, a kind of fatigue in which your eyes feel tired, your head aches, and words on the screen appear blurry. Fortunately, this discomfort is usually temporary and disappears with rest.

While you concentrate on a screen, you also blink considerably less often than usual. Blinking spreads a thin film of tears that preserves the moisture of your eyes, so reduced blinking can leave them dry, itchy, and irritated.

Eye doctors recommend the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something approximately 6 meters away for 20 seconds. Gazing into the distance allows the focusing muscles to relax.

Time outdoors is important as well. Myopia, or nearsightedness, makes distant objects look blurry, and it is becoming far more common among children around the world. It often develops when the eyeball grows slightly too long. Research indicates that children who spend time outside every day, in natural daylight, are less likely to develop myopia.

Finally, switch off screens about an hour before bedtime. Bright light in the evening can reduce melatonin, a substance your body produces to signal that it is time to sleep, which makes it more difficult to fall asleep.

Screens are remarkably helpful tools, so simply use them wisely and give your eyes regular breaks.

versions.title: Eyes and Screens: Protecting Your Vision in a Digital World
versions.text:
Phones, tablets, computers, and televisions have become an essential part of contemporary life, and many students now spend several hours each day looking at screens for schoolwork, entertainment, and communication. Screens are undeniably valuable tools, but your eyes require particular attention when you use them for extended periods.

To understand why, it helps to know how your eyes function. Light enters through the pupil, the dark opening in the center of each eye, and a transparent lens bends that light so that it lands precisely on the retina, a delicate layer of sensitive cells lining the back of the eye. The retina converts the light into electrical signals, which travel along the optic nerve to your brain, where they are assembled into the image you perceive.

To see objects up close, your eyes must focus, so tiny muscles inside each eye contract to adjust the curvature of the lens. Because a screen is typically held close to your face, these muscles remain active continuously, and eventually you may experience digital eye strain, a form of fatigue in which your eyes feel tired, your head aches, and words on the screen appear blurry, although fortunately this discomfort is usually temporary and disappears with adequate rest.

While you concentrate on a screen, you also blink considerably less frequently than usual. Blinking distributes a thin film of tears that preserves the moisture of your eyes, so reduced blinking can leave them dry, itchy, and irritated.

Eye doctors recommend the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something approximately 6 meters away for 20 seconds. Gazing into the distance allows the focusing muscles to relax completely.

Time outdoors is significant as well. Myopia, or nearsightedness, causes distant objects to look blurry, and it is becoming dramatically more common among children worldwide. It frequently develops when the eyeball grows slightly too long, so that light focuses in front of the retina instead of directly on it. Research indicates that children who spend time outside every day, in natural daylight, are less likely to develop myopia.

Finally, switch off screens approximately an hour before bedtime. Bright light in the evening can reduce melatonin, a hormone your body produces to signal that it is time to sleep, which makes falling asleep more difficult.

Screens are remarkably helpful tools, so use them thoughtfully and give your eyes regular breaks.

versions.title: Eyes and Screens: Protecting Your Vision in a Digital World
versions.text:
Phones, tablets, computers, and televisions have become an indispensable part of contemporary life, and many students now spend several hours each day looking at screens for schoolwork, entertainment, and communication. Screens are undeniably valuable tools, but your eyes require particular attention when you use them for extended periods.

To understand why, it helps to know how your eyes function. Light enters through the pupil, the dark opening in the center of each eye, and a transparent lens refracts that light so that it lands precisely on the retina, a delicate layer of light-sensitive cells lining the back of the eye. The retina converts the light into electrical signals, which travel along the optic nerve to your brain, where they are assembled into the image you perceive.

To see objects up close, your eyes must focus, so tiny muscles inside each eye contract to adjust the curvature of the lens. Because a screen is typically positioned close to your face, these muscles remain active continuously, and eventually you may experience digital eye strain, a form of fatigue in which your eyes feel exhausted, your head aches, and text on the screen appears blurry, although fortunately this discomfort is usually temporary and disappears with adequate rest.

While you concentrate intensely on a screen, you also blink considerably less frequently than usual. Blinking distributes a thin film of tears that preserves the moisture of your eyes, so diminished blinking can leave them dry, itchy, and irritated.

Optometrists recommend the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something approximately 6 meters away for 20 seconds. Gazing into the distance allows the focusing muscles to relax completely.

Time outdoors is significant as well. Myopia, or nearsightedness, causes distant objects to look blurry, and it is becoming dramatically more prevalent among children worldwide. The condition frequently develops when the eyeball grows slightly too long, so that incoming light focuses in front of the retina instead of directly on it. Research indicates that children who spend time outside every day, exposed to natural daylight, are considerably less likely to develop myopia.

Finally, switch off screens approximately an hour before bedtime, because bright illumination in the evening can suppress melatonin, a hormone your body produces to signal that it is time to sleep, which makes falling asleep more difficult.

Screens are remarkably beneficial instruments, so use them thoughtfully and give your eyes regular, deliberate breaks.

The retina converts the light into electrical signals, which travel along the optic nerve to your brain, where they are interpreted and assembled into the image you perceive.

questions.stem: What is the job of the optic nerve?
options: It carries signals from the retina to the brain.
It bends light onto the retina.
It controls how often you blink.
It produces tears for the eye.
questions.why: The article states that electrical signals from the retina travel along the optic nerve to the brain.

wrong.C: The article does not link the optic nerve to blinking.
wrong.D: The article does not say the optic nerve makes tears.

questions.stem: The article describes digital eye strain as a kind of fatigue. What does fatigue mean?
options: Strong excitement
Great tiredness
Sharp eyesight
Sudden hunger
questions.why: The article explains that eye strain makes the eyes feel tired or exhausted, which is what fatigue means.

wrong.A: Fatigue is the opposite of excitement.
wrong.C: Eye strain makes vision blurry, not sharp.
wrong.D: Hunger is not mentioned.

questions.stem: What chain of events leads to dry eyes during screen use?
options: Bright light from the screen heats the eye, which slowly melts the lens.
The pupil closes, which stops tears from forming.
The eyeball grows too long, which squeezes out water.
Concentration reduces blinking, so less moisture spreads.
questions.why: The article explains that people blink less while concentrating, and blinking spreads the tears that keep eyes moist.

wrong.A: The article does not say screens heat or melt the eye.
wrong.B: The pupil lets light in; it does not control tears.
wrong.C: A longer eyeball is linked to myopia, not dry eyes.

questions.stem: Why does the 20-20-20 rule require looking at an object about 6 meters away rather than one nearby?
options: Distant objects are brighter than screens.
It lets the focusing muscles relax.
Nearby objects produce melatonin.
The retina cannot detect objects that are close.
questions.why: Muscles contract to focus up close, so looking into the distance gives them a chance to relax.

wrong.A: Brightness is not the reason given.
wrong.D: The retina detects close objects; the problem is muscle effort.

questions.stem: How is digital eye strain different from myopia, according to the article?
options: Eye strain is permanent, but myopia goes away with sleep.
Eye strain affects only adults, but myopia affects only animals and never people.
Eye strain is usually temporary; myopia is a lasting change in eye shape.
Both are caused only by a lack of melatonin.
questions.why: The article says eye strain usually disappears with rest, while myopia develops when the eyeball grows slightly too long.

wrong.A: This reverses the facts in the article.
wrong.B: The article discusses both conditions in children and students.
wrong.D: Melatonin is linked to sleep, not to these conditions.

questions.stem: Why does the author begin by calling screens valuable tools before describing their effects?
options: To present a balanced view that screens are useful but need sensible habits
To convince readers to buy more screens
To show that screens have no effects on the eyes
To introduce a story about a famous inventor
questions.why: The author recognizes that screens are helpful, then explains how to use them wisely, which gives a balanced view.

wrong.B: The article does not advertise screens.
wrong.C: The article goes on to describe strain, dryness, and sleep problems.
wrong.D: No inventor is mentioned.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say screens are bad for children's eyes. Using evidence from the article, explain whether you agree, and describe which habits matter most for protecting vision.
checklist: I stated a clear opinion about screens and eye health.
I supported my opinion with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I used precise vocabulary from the article and organized my answer in clear paragraphs.
